questions.knowledge_point: Identifying True Statements Regarding Interiors and Boundaries of Sets
questions.problem:
Consider the set $A,$ defined by 

$$
A={(x,y)\in {R}^{2}\,:\,y<1-x}.
$$

Which of the following statements are true?

- $A$ contains all of its boundary points.
- $A$ contains none of its boundary points.
- $\text{int}\,A=A$
questions.worked_solution:
The boundary of a set $A,$ denoted $∂A,$ is the set that contains all the boundary points of $A.$

In this case, the set $A$ and its boundary $∂A$ are shown below.

![](/home/jake/Developer/Course_Academy/reference/mathacademy/question-capture-workers/multivariable/14053801/assets/5151df3c5b84ffaca9aa16b401cd9364fea10a240d39c9c28d815b36e417b16d.png)

The interior of a set $A,$ denoted $\text{int}\,A,$ is the set containing all the interior points of $A.$ It contains every point in $A$ except the boundary points: 

$$
\text{int}\,A=A-∂A
$$

Notice that, in this case, the set $A$ contains none of its boundary points. 

With that in mind, let's examine each statement:

- Statement I is false, while statement II is true. As we've seen, $A$ contains none of its boundary points.

- Statement III is true. Since $A$ contains none of its boundary points, we must have $\text{int}\,A=A.$

Therefore, the correct answer is "II and III only."

choices.value: None of the statements are true.

questions.problem:
Consider the set $A,$ defined by 

$$
A={(x,y)\in {R}^{2}\,:\,1<{x}^{2}+{y}^{2}\le 4}.
$$

Which of the following statements are true?

- $A$ contains none of its boundary points.
- $A$ contains some (not all) of its boundary points.
- $\text{int}\,A=A$
questions.worked_solution:
The boundary of a set $A,$ denoted $∂A,$ is the set that contains all the boundary points of $A.$

In this case, the set $A$ and its boundary $∂A$ are shown below.

![](/home/jake/Developer/Course_Academy/reference/mathacademy/question-capture-workers/multivariable/14053801/assets/8414de2e05da43c03fae3c8b1ff2102401e990188e9fd4ee59a24308ec34b086.png)

 

The interior of a set $A,$ denoted $\text{int}\,A,$ is the set containing all the interior points of $A.$ It contains every point in $A$ except the boundary points: 

$$
\text{int}\,A=A-∂A
$$

Notice that, in this case, the set $A$ contains some (not all) of its boundary points.

With that in mind, let's examine each statement:

- Statement I is false, while statement II is true. As we have seen, $∂A$ consists of two concentric circles: the outer one is in $A,$ while the inner one is not.

- Statement III is false. Since $A$ contains some of its boundary points, we must have $\text{int}\,A\ne A.$

Therefore, the correct answer is "II only."

Consider the set $A$ shown above. The interior of $A$ is 

$$
\text{int}\,A={(x,y)\in {R}^{2}\,:\,0<x<2,\,}.
$$

What is the missing expression?
questions.worked_solution:
The boundary of a set $A,$ denoted $∂A,$ is the set that contains all the boundary points of $A.$

The set $A$ and its boundary $∂A$ are shown below.

![](/home/jake/Developer/Course_Academy/reference/mathacademy/question-capture-workers/multivariable/14053801/assets/0a0b92621d83d6395926a75b5cae34f479a8b9e64dfe82711094c3724b3b3220.png)

The interior of a set $A,$ denoted $\text{int}\,A,$ is the set containing all the interior points of $A.$ It contains every point in $A$ except the boundary points: 

$$
\text{int}\,A=A-∂A
$$

The interior of $A$ is shown below.

![](/home/jake/Developer/Course_Academy/reference/mathacademy/question-capture-workers/multivariable/14053801/assets/3ddef68bf4b4284c1b68896920fddb8d7fb0e70eba15dee103cdbc0134a9ed20.png)

So, in this case, the interior of $A$ is given by
